notes:
Chemical equilibrium

  • Dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations become constant (not zero change, but no net change).
  • Law of mass action: for $aA+bB \rightleftharpoons cC+dD$, $K_c = \dfrac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$; $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$.
  • $K \gg 1$: reaction goes to completion (product favoured); $K \ll 1$: reactant favoured. $K$ for reverse reaction $= 1/K$. If a reaction is multiplied by $n$, new $K = K^n$.

Le Chatelier's principle

If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to partially oppose the change.

ChangeEffect
↑ Concentration of reactantshifts forward
↑ Pressure (↓ volume)shifts toward fewer gas moles
↑ Temperatureshifts endothermic direction
Catalystno shift; only speeds up attainment of equilibrium
Inert gas at constant volumeno effect on equilibrium

Ionic equilibrium: acids & bases

  • Arrhenius: acid gives H$^+$, base gives OH$^-$ in water. Bronsted-Lowry: acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor (conjugate acid-base pairs differ by one H$^+$). Lewis: acid = electron-pair acceptor, base = electron-pair donor.
  • $K_w = [H^+][OH^-] = 10^{-14}$ at 25°C. $pH = -\log[H^+]$; $pOH = -\log[OH^-]$; $pH + pOH = 14$.
  • Weak acid: $[H^+] = \sqrt{K_a C}$, degree of dissociation $\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}$ (Ostwald's dilution law). Weak base similarly with $K_b$.
  • $pK_a = -\log K_a$; $pK_a + pK_b = 14$ for a conjugate pair.

Buffer solutions

Resist change in pH on small addition of acid/base. Henderson-Hasselbalch: $pH = pK_a + \log\dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}$ (acidic buffer, e.g. CH$_3$COOH + CH$_3$COONa); $pOH = pK_b + \log\dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{base}]}$ (basic buffer, e.g. NH$_4$OH + NH$_4$Cl). Maximum buffer capacity when $[\text{salt}]=[\text{acid}]$, i.e. $pH = pK_a$.

Salt hydrolysis

Salt typeNature
Strong acid + strong base (NaCl)neutral, no hydrolysis
Strong acid + weak base (NH$_4$Cl)acidic
Weak acid + strong base (CH$_3$COONa)basic
Weak acid + weak base (CH$_3$COONH$_4$)depends on $K_a$ vs $K_b$

Exam tip

3–4 questions: $K_c$/$K_p$ relation, Le Chatelier shift direction, weak acid pH/Ostwald numerical, buffer pH via Henderson-Hasselbalch, and a $K_{sp}$-solubility numerical. Master $\log$ values (0.301, 0.477, 0.699).

questions.q: At chemical equilibrium,
options: the rate constants of forward and reverse reactions are equal
the concentrations of reactants and products no longer change with time
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is dynamic: both forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant, not zero net reaction.
questions.trick: Dynamic equilibrium: rates equal, concentrations constant — reaction never actually stops.

questions.q: The relation between $K_p$ and $K_c$ for a gaseous reaction is
questions.explanation: Derived from ideal gas law substitution into the equilibrium expression; when $\Delta n_g = 0$, $K_p = K_c$.
questions.trick: $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$; if $\Delta n_g=0$, they're equal.

questions.q: For the reaction $N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$, $\Delta H < 0$. Increasing temperature will
options: shift equilibrium backward, decreasing NH$_3$ yield
shift equilibrium forward only at high pressure
shift equilibrium forward, increasing NH$_3$ yield
questions.explanation: Since the forward reaction is exothermic, raising temperature (adding heat) shifts equilibrium in the endothermic (reverse) direction, per Le Chatelier's principle.
questions.trick: Exothermic forward → heating favours the reverse (endothermic) direction.

questions.q: Increasing pressure on the equilibrium $N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$ will
options: shift it forward only at low temperature
questions.explanation: 4 mol gas → 2 mol gas; increasing pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas, i.e. the forward direction.
questions.trick: More pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles.

questions.q: Addition of a catalyst to a reaction at equilibrium
options: does not shift equilibrium, only speeds up attaining it
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers activation energy for both forward and reverse reactions equally, helping equilibrium to be reached faster without changing its position or $K$.
questions.trick: Catalyst speeds both directions equally — no shift, no change in $K$.

questions.q: The pH of a $10^{-3}$ M HCl solution is
questions.explanation: HCl is a strong acid, fully dissociated: $[H^+] = 10^{-3}$ M, so $pH = -\log(10^{-3}) = 3$.
questions.trick: Strong acid fully dissociates: $pH = -\log[H^+]$ directly from concentration.

questions.q: The degree of dissociation of a weak acid according to Ostwald's dilution law is given by
questions.explanation: $K_a = C\alpha^2$ (for small $\alpha$), so $\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}$ — degree of dissociation increases on dilution (decreasing $C$).
questions.trick: Ostwald: $\alpha=\sqrt{K_a/C}$ — dissociation rises as concentration falls.

questions.q: A 0.01 M solution of a weak acid HA has $K_a = 1\times10^{-6}$. Its pH is approximately
questions.trick: $[H^+]=\sqrt{K_aC}$ for a weak acid — plug in and take $-\log$.

questions.q: According to the Bronsted-Lowry concept, a base is defined as a species that
questions.explanation: Bronsted-Lowry base = proton acceptor; the corresponding acid is a proton donor. (Electron pair donor/acceptor is the Lewis definition.)
questions.trick: Bronsted-Lowry base = proton acceptor (not electron-pair donor — that's Lewis).

questions.q: An acidic buffer solution can be prepared by mixing
questions.explanation: A weak acid (CH$_3$COOH) with its salt of a strong base (CH$_3$COONa) forms an acidic buffer. NH$_4$OH+NH$_4$Cl is a basic buffer.
questions.trick: Weak acid + its salt of a strong base = classic acidic buffer.

questions.q: For an acidic buffer, the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is
questions.explanation: Standard Henderson-Hasselbalch relation for a weak acid buffer.
questions.trick: Henderson-Hasselbalch: $pH = pK_a + \log([\text{salt}]/[\text{acid}])$.

questions.q: A buffer of 0.1 M CH$_3$COOH and 0.1 M CH$_3$COONa has $pK_a = 4.74$. Its pH is
questions.explanation: Since [salt] = [acid], $\log(1) = 0$, so $pH = pK_a = 4.74$ — buffer capacity is maximum here.
questions.trick: Equal salt and acid → $\log(1)=0$ → $pH = pK_a$ exactly.

questions.q: An aqueous solution of ammonium chloride (NH$_4$Cl) is
questions.explanation: NH$_4$Cl is a salt of a weak base (NH$_4$OH) and strong acid (HCl); the NH$_4^+$ ion hydrolyses to give an acidic solution.
questions.trick: Weak base + strong acid salt (NH$_4$Cl) → cation hydrolyses → acidic.

questions.q: The solubility product expression for Ag$_2$CrO$_4$ (which dissociates as Ag$_2$CrO$_4 \rightleftharpoons 2Ag^+ + CrO_4^{2-}$) is
questions.explanation: $K_{sp} = [Ag^+]^2[CrO_4^{2-}]$, powers equal to stoichiometric coefficients.
questions.trick: $K_{sp}$ powers match stoichiometric coefficients: $[Ag^+]^2[CrO_4^{2-}]$.

questions.q: If the solubility of AgCl is $s$ mol L$^{-1}$, its $K_{sp}$ is
questions.explanation: AgCl $\rightleftharpoons Ag^+ + Cl^-$; $[Ag^+]=[Cl^-]=s$, so $K_{sp} = s\times s = s^2$.
questions.trick: 1:1 salt: $K_{sp}=s^2$ when both ions come from one formula unit.

questions.q: Common ion effect on the solubility of a sparingly soluble salt
options: converts it to a strong electrolyte
questions.explanation: Adding a common ion shifts the dissolution equilibrium backward (Le Chatelier), decreasing solubility, e.g. adding NaCl decreases AgCl solubility.
questions.trick: Common ion pushes dissolution equilibrium backward — solubility always drops.

questions.q: The pH of pure water at 25°C is 7 because
options: water does not ionise at all
questions.explanation: Water self-ionises slightly: $[H^+][OH^-]=10^{-14}$; since they're equal, each is $10^{-7}$ M, giving pH 7 (neutral).
questions.trick: $K_w=[H^+][OH^-]=10^{-14}$; equal split gives $10^{-7}$ each → pH 7.

questions.q: A solution has $pOH = 4$. Its pH is
questions.explanation: $pH + pOH = 14 \Rightarrow pH = 14 - 4 = 10$.
questions.trick: $pH+pOH=14$ always at 25°C — just subtract.

questions.q: If $K_a$ of an acid is $10^{-5}$, its $pK_a$ and conjugate base's $pK_b$ are
questions.explanation: $pK_a = -\log(10^{-5}) = 5$. Since $pK_a + pK_b = 14$ for a conjugate pair, $pK_b = 14 - 5 = 9$.
questions.trick: $pK_a+pK_b=14$ for a conjugate pair; compute $pK_a$ first, subtract from 14.

questions.q: For a reaction at equilibrium, if the reaction quotient $Q < K_c$, then
options: the system is already at equilibrium
the reaction proceeds forward to reach equilibrium
the reaction proceeds backward to reach equilibrium
questions.explanation: When $Q < K$, there is a relative excess of reactants, so the reaction moves forward (more products form) until $Q$ equals $K$.
questions.trick: $Q<K$ means excess reactant → reaction runs forward to catch up.

questions.q: For $PCl_5(g) \rightleftharpoons PCl_3(g) + Cl_2(g)$, $K_c = 1.8$ at 500 K. The value of $K_p$ is (R = 0.0821 L atm K$^{-1}$mol$^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: $\Delta n_g = 2-1 = 1$; $K_p = K_c(RT)^1 = 1.8\times0.0821\times500 \approx 73.9$.
questions.trick: $K_p=K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$; here $\Delta n_g=1$, so multiply by $RT$ once.

questions.q: Addition of an inert gas at constant volume to a gaseous equilibrium
options: has no effect on the equilibrium position
questions.explanation: At constant volume, adding an inert gas does not change the partial pressures or concentrations of the reacting species, so the equilibrium position is unaffected.
questions.trick: Inert gas at constant volume doesn't change partial pressures — no shift.

questions.q: Addition of an inert gas at constant pressure to the equilibrium $N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$
options: shifts it backward, decreasing NH$_3$ yield
questions.explanation: At constant pressure, adding inert gas increases the total volume, which lowers the partial pressures of all reacting gases — equivalent to decreasing pressure, so equilibrium shifts toward the side with more gas moles (backward here).
questions.trick: Inert gas at constant pressure dilutes the gases like lowering pressure — shifts toward more gas moles.

questions.q: Which of the following is a Lewis acid?
questions.explanation: BF$_3$ has an incomplete octet on boron and can accept an electron pair, making it a Lewis acid; the others are electron-pair donors (Lewis bases).
questions.trick: Lewis acid accepts an electron pair; incomplete octet (BF$_3$) is the giveaway.

questions.q: Which of the following species is amphiprotic (can act as both a Bronsted acid and base)?
questions.explanation: HCO$_3^-$ can donate a proton (to form CO$_3^{2-}$) or accept one (to form H$_2$CO$_3$), so it is amphiprotic.
questions.trick: Amphiprotic species can both gain and lose a proton — look for an -HCO$_3^-$-type ion.

questions.q: A 0.01 M solution of NH$_4$OH has $K_b = 1\times10^{-6}$. Its pH is approximately
questions.trick: $[OH^-]=\sqrt{K_bC}$ for a weak base; convert $pOH$ to $pH$ via 14 minus.

questions.q: Adding solid CH$_3$COONa to a CH$_3$COOH solution
options: increases the degree of ionisation of CH$_3$COOH
has no effect on the degree of ionisation
decreases the degree of ionisation of CH$_3$COOH (common ion effect)
questions.explanation: The acetate ion from CH$_3$COONa is common to the acid's dissociation equilibrium; by Le Chatelier's principle it suppresses further ionisation of CH$_3$COOH.
questions.trick: Adding the salt's common ion suppresses the weak acid's own ionisation.

questions.q: The molar solubility of AgCl in water, given $K_{sp} = 1.8\times10^{-10}$, is
questions.explanation: $K_{sp} = s^2 \Rightarrow s = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-10}} \approx 1.34\times10^{-5}$ M.
questions.trick: 1:1 salt: $s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}$ — simple square root, no factors needed.

questions.q: The solubility of AgCl ($K_{sp} = 1.8\times10^{-10}$) in 0.1 M NaCl solution is approximately
questions.explanation: With a common ion, $[Cl^-] \approx 0.1$ M (from NaCl); $s = K_{sp}/[Cl^-] = 1.8\times10^{-10}/0.1 = 1.8\times10^{-9}$ M — much lower solubility than in pure water (common ion effect).
questions.trick: Common ion effect: $s \approx K_{sp}/[\text{common ion}]$, not $\sqrt{K_{sp}}$.

questions.q: If the ionic product of a sparingly soluble salt in solution exceeds its $K_{sp}$,
questions.explanation: When the ionic product exceeds $K_{sp}$, the solution is supersaturated, and excess solid precipitates out until the ionic product equals $K_{sp}$.
questions.trick: Ionic product $> K_{sp}$ means supersaturated → excess solid precipitates.

questions.q: The equilibrium constant $K$ of a reaction changes only with a change in
questions.explanation: $K$ depends only on temperature; catalysts, concentration and pressure changes shift the position of equilibrium but leave $K$ unchanged at a given $T$.
questions.trick: $K$ changes with temperature only — catalyst/pressure/concentration never touch it.

questions.q: For $H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)$, $K_c = 50$. At an instant, $[H_2]=[I_2]=0.1$ M and $[HI]=0.4$ M. The reaction will proceed
options: the system is already at equilibrium
questions.explanation: $Q_c = (0.4)^2/(0.1\times0.1) = 16$, which is less than $K_c = 50$, so the reaction proceeds forward to form more HI until $Q_c = K_c$.
questions.trick: Compute $Q_c$ from given concentrations, compare to $K_c$ to find direction.

questions.q: For an endothermic reaction, increasing the temperature causes the equilibrium constant $K$ to
questions.explanation: Raising temperature favours the endothermic (heat-absorbing) direction; since the forward reaction is endothermic here, more products form, increasing $K$.
questions.trick: Endothermic forward reaction: heating increases $K$, favouring products.

questions.q: On diluting a weak acid solution 100 times, its degree of dissociation ($\alpha$)
questions.explanation: By Ostwald's dilution law, $\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}$, so $\alpha \propto 1/\sqrt{C}$; diluting 100 times increases $\alpha$ by a factor of $\sqrt{100} = 10$.
questions.trick: $\alpha \propto 1/\sqrt{C}$; diluting 100$\times$ raises $\alpha$ by $\sqrt{100}=10\times$.

questions.q: The pH of a 0.001 M NaOH solution is
questions.explanation: NaOH is a strong base: $[OH^-] = 10^{-3}$ M, $pOH = 3$, so $pH = 14-3 = 11$.
questions.trick: Strong base fully dissociates: get $pOH$ from $[OH^-]$, then $pH=14-pOH$.

questions.q: A buffer is prepared with 0.2 mol CH$_3$COOH and 0.1 mol CH$_3$COONa in 1 L solution ($pK_a = 4.74$). Its pH is
questions.trick: Henderson-Hasselbalch with unequal moles: $pH=pK_a+\log(\text{salt/acid ratio})$.

questions.q: Which of the following salts gives a neutral aqueous solution?
questions.explanation: NaCl is a salt of a strong acid (HCl) and a strong base (NaOH); neither ion hydrolyses, so the solution remains neutral.
questions.trick: Strong acid + strong base salt hydrolyses not at all → stays neutral.

questions.q: In an aqueous solution of CH$_3$COONH$_4$, if $K_a$(CH$_3$COOH) = $K_b$(NH$_4$OH), the solution is
questions.explanation: For a salt of a weak acid and weak base, the solution's nature depends on the relative strengths of $K_a$ and $K_b$; if they are equal, the hydrolysis exactly balances and the solution is neutral.
questions.trick: Weak acid + weak base salt: equal $K_a$ and $K_b$ cancel out to neutral.

questions.q: For the equilibrium $2SO_2(g) + O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2SO_3(g)$, the relation between $K_p$ and $K_c$ is
questions.trick: Compute $\Delta n_g$ (products − reactants) first, then apply $K_p=K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$.

questions.q: For a reaction at a given instant, if the reaction quotient $Q$ is greater than $K_c$, the reaction will proceed
questions.explanation: When $Q > K$, there is a relative excess of products, so the reaction shifts in the reverse direction until $Q$ decreases to equal $K$.
questions.trick: $Q>K$ means excess product → reaction runs backward to catch up.
